newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU's cotton row spotlights disputed dumping policy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU's cotton row spotlights disputed dumping policy.

text.p: Recent European Union wrangling over proposed anti-dumping duties on cotton exports from six developing states has spotlighted the bloc's external trade tactics and pitched its northern free trader states against the rest.

The row, which is set to rumble on as the European Commission ponders its response to new trade data from EU cotton producers, centres on the case for duties on unbleached cotton from China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Turkey and Pakistan.
EU foreign ministers threw out the Commission's dumping proposal in late May, delighting or infuriating those involved depending on their trade ideology.

The ministers' decision also raised the temperature in a review of EU anti-dumping rules, which the Commission has suggested should be applied with more attention to EU consumer and consumer industry interests as well as those of producing industries.

The Commission says its anti-dumping policy aims to counter unfair trade practices which damage EU industry, activities such as non-EU countries' use of protected home markets to subsidise knock-down prices for their exports to the bloc.

Supporters say anti-dumping laws are essential defence against exports from protected markets while opponents, usually poorer countries, see them as weapons allowing richer countries to protect their markets by beating back cheaper imports.
EU ATTACKED FOR ARBITRARY DECISIONS

While the EU trails the United States in terms of dumping actions, with 171 underway as of June 30, 1996 compared with Washington's 307, it comes in for more flak on dumping policy because of the apparently arbitary way it takes some decisions.
The cotton case was just such an instance, said one Commission official, who accused ministers of acting unlawfully and politically in ignoring arguments for definitive duties.
"The problem we see is not so much a problem of our own legislation but a problem... which is to do with politicians. We cannot do anything about it," added the official, who asked not to be named.

While some say the European Council of Ministers erred in letting duties drop, the alternative could also have brought legal action, according to Brian Hindley, reader in trade policy at the London School of Economics.
"If the Council had imposed definitive duties, there would surely have been a case in the WTO and the duties would almost certainly have been struck down," he said.
Hindley attacked the European Commission's calculation of cotton dumping margins and what he said was its failure to prove a link between the dumping and injury suffered by EU industry.

"I think their determination of dumping margins violated the WTO (World Trade Organisation) rules," he said, adding that the existence of thousands of cotton fabric firms in the targeted countries meant the idea of them fixing prices was a joke.
COMPLEXITY OF ISSUES
Hindley said existing EU cotton quotas limited the scope for imports to hit domestic producers' market share, throwing doubt on any proven link between dumping and injury.
"To say the dumping caused injury is extremely dodgy. It would have been extremely interesting to see the Community defend itself in the WTO. The case was shot through with illegality," he said.

The Commission official disagreed on both counts, saying that dumping did not depend only on price fixing and the existence of quotas did not mean EU producers were fully protected from the effects of that dumping.

Descending into the depths of argument and counter-argument on cotton duties, properly the territory of the trade lawyers who profit from such matters, shows only the complexity of the issues rather than who is necessarily right or wrong.
Domestic producers want any protection they can get while consumers want goods at the cheapest possible prices -- which is where the guidelines on European Community interest come in.

The Commission proposal, set to be finalised in the coming weeks, is that consumers and consuming industries be alerted early during dumping inquiries to allow them to say how eventual measures might damage their interests.

It would then be for Commission officials to decide the case for duties, having weighed whether the negative impact of measures would be "clearly disproportionate" to the likely benefits, a balance which is left to officials' discretion.

"This is something which has to be seen on a case-by-case basis. We have not got anything in the form of a formula into which we could put a couple of economic indicators and then get a result. It will remain a matter of judgement," the official said, adding that guidelines would have some precedent value but no legally binding effect.
DUMPING INSTRUMENT DRAWS FIRE

Even such apparently anodyne adjustments have proved too much for EU employers' organisation UNICE, which warned in April that few bar Canada among the EU's trading partners had the equivalent of Community interest provisions.
But for Philip von Schoeppenthau, trade adviser at EuroCommerce, the European retailers and wholesalers' body, the plan offers hope of relief from higher import prices.

"We very much welcome the new guidelines on Community interest. Our view is that the anti-dumping instrument is biased against consumers and the consuming sectors, people like EuroCommerce and people who want to import things," he said.
With such divisions within the EU itself, it is hardly surprising the dumping instrument draws fire from abroad.
For Hindley, the whole dumping issue would be better dealt with as an anti-trust problem, using sanctions against those companies who abuse their dominant position.

"There are laws to deal with one firm disadvantaging another by charging low prices. If the firm doing this is in a dominant position we can take action," he said, adding that such a tactic could cut out 80 or 90 percent of current cases.
Not such a far-fetched idea, said the Commission official, who added that it was unlikely to happen any time soon.
"The ideal situation would be a world-wide single market with a world-wide department of justice applying world-wide competition rules. Anti-dumping is a second best solution for a non-ideal world."
